set.detail:
The Perusine War (41-40) arose from the settlement of veterans after Philippi. Octavian, responsible for Italy, confiscated land from eighteen cities and many individuals for some 50,000 or more veterans. The dispossessed protested, and the veterans demanded more. Lucius Antonius, consul in 41 and brother of Mark Antony, and Fulvia, Antony's wife, presented themselves as champions of the Italians against Octavian's illegal confiscations and as protectors of Antony's interests, perhaps fearing Octavian's growing power while Antony was in the East.

Mediation by officers and veterans failed. In late 41 Lucius occupied Rome briefly, then retreated north toward Antony's generals in Gaul, Ventidius, Pollio and Plancus, who hesitated to commit themselves without Antony's orders. Octavian's generals, Agrippa and Salvidienus Rufus, trapped Lucius in Perusia (Perugia) in Etruria, which Octavian besieged through the winter, building a wall and ditch around the town. Lead sling bullets with obscene inscriptions survive from the siege. Starvation forced Lucius to surrender in early 40.

Octavian pardoned Lucius and his troops, but executed the town council and, according to hostile sources, sacrificed 300 senators and equites at an altar of Divus Iulius on the Ides of March. The town burned. Fulvia fled to Greece, where she died. Antony's generals withdrew; Octavian took over Gaul and its legions after the death of its governor Calenus.

The war almost caused open conflict between Antony and Octavian, averted by the Treaty of Brundisium in autumn 40. It consolidated Octavian's control of Italy and the West.

Sextus Pompeius, younger son of Pompey the Great, escaped from Munda and built a naval power in the western Mediterranean. Outlawed by the lex Pedia in 43 and proscribed, he received a command of the fleet from the Senate in 43, then seized Sicily, which became a refuge for proscribed men and runaway slaves. With a large fleet commanded by freedmen such as Menodorus and Menecrates, he blockaded Italy, causing famine in Rome. He called himself son of Neptune.

The Treaty of Misenum in 39 recognised his control of Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and the Peloponnese, in return for ending the blockade; the proscribed were allowed to return. But in 38 Menodorus defected with Sardinia, and war resumed. Octavian's fleet was defeated off Cumae and wrecked by a storm at Scyllaeum. Agrippa built a new fleet in 37, at the Portus Julius, training 20,000 rowers; Antony provided 120 ships at Tarentum.

In 36 a triple invasion of Sicily began. Octavian was defeated off Tauromenium, but Agrippa won at Mylae and decisively at Naulochus on 3 September 36. Sextus fled to Asia, where he was killed in 35. Lepidus, who had landed in Sicily with twelve legions, tried to claim the island, but his army deserted to Octavian, who deposed him from the triumvirate.

Octavian presented the war as a war against pirates and slaves, returning 30,000 slaves to their owners and crucifying 6,000 more. The victory secured Italy's grain supply and Octavian's popularity, earned him tribunician sacrosanctity, and left him master of the West. Modern scholars (Powell, Welch) have rehabilitated Sextus as a Republican leader rather than a mere pirate.

scholarship: Powell, Sextus Pompeius (2002)

set.detail:
Antony's Parthian war began with the Parthian invasion of 40, when Pacorus and Quintus Labienus overran Syria, Asia Minor and Judaea while Antony was in Egypt and Italy. His legate Publius Ventidius Bassus drove them out in 39, defeating and killing Labienus at the Cilician Gates and Pharnapates at the Amanus, and in 38 killed Pacorus at Gindarus. Herod, named king by the Senate, recovered Judaea with Sosius in 37.

Antony then prepared a great invasion to realise Caesar's plan of revenge for Carrhae. In 36, with sixteen legions and allies, about 100,000 men, he marched through Armenia to Media Atropatene. Phraates IV destroyed his siege train, Artavasdes of Armenia withdrew, and Antony failed to take Phraaspa. His retreat through the mountains in winter cost some 24,000 men. In 35 the Median king, quarrelling with Parthia, became Antony's ally; in 34 Antony captured Artavasdes of Armenia, annexing the kingdom, and celebrated in Alexandria, followed by the Donations. He betrothed his son Alexander Helios to the Median princess Iotape.

The Parthian campaign was a costly failure, though Antony salvaged Armenia. In Rome Octavian concealed and exploited it, contrasting it with his own victories over Sextus Pompey and in Illyricum. Antony's dependence on Cleopatra's resources after 36 fed Octavian's propaganda.

The war shows the difficulty of attacking Parthia across mountains and desert, and the limits of Roman power in the East. It ended with Antony's defeat at Actium; Armenia was lost again. Augustus recovered Crassus' standards by diplomacy in 20 BC, a settlement that lasted for generations.

scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)

set.detail:
Between 35 and 33 Octavian campaigned in Illyricum, partly to secure Italy's north-eastern frontier, partly to train his army, and partly to win military glory to compare with Antony's eastern campaigns. In 35 he attacked the Iapydes in the Julian Alps, storming their towns Terponus and Metulum, where he was wounded leading the assault and the defenders burned themselves with their families. He then marched into Pannonia, besieged and took Siscia (Sisak) on the Save, and left a garrison of twenty-five cohorts there.

In 34 and 33 he turned against the Dalmatae, who had destroyed Gabinius' army in 48 and held its standards. He was wounded again at Setovia; Promona and other strongholds fell. The Dalmatae surrendered in 33, returning the standards and providing hostages. His generals Agrippa, Statilius Taurus and Messalla campaigned against the Salassi and other Alpine tribes and the Liburnian pirates.

The campaigns were well publicised in Rome. Octavian displayed the recovered standards in the Porticus Octaviae, built from the spoils; Agrippa, aedile in 33, spent lavishly on Rome's water supply and public works. In 29 Octavian celebrated the first of his three triumphs, for Illyricum.

The Illyrian war gave Octavian military credentials and secured the land route between Italy and the Balkans. It laid the foundations for the later conquest of Pannonia and the Danube frontier under Augustus and Tiberius. Appian's Illyrian book, based on Augustus' memoirs, gives a detailed account, which inflates Octavian's achievements.

scholarship: Wilkes, Dalmatia (1969)
Šašel Kos, Appian and Illyricum (2005)

set.detail:
The War of Actium (32-30) was the final civil war of the Republic, between Octavian and Mark Antony with Cleopatra. Relations had worsened since 36: Octavian deposed Lepidus and took his provinces, refused Antony recruits, and attacked his relationship with Cleopatra and the Donations of Alexandria (34). The triumvirate's legal basis expired at the end of 33. In 32 the consuls and some 300 senators fled to Antony; Antony divorced Octavia; Octavian published his will. War was declared on Cleopatra alone, presenting it as a foreign war, after all Italy swore an oath to Octavian.

Antony gathered about 500 warships and nineteen legions in western Greece, with bases from Corcyra to Methone. In 31 Agrippa seized Methone, Leucas, Patrae and Corinth, cutting Antony's supply lines from Egypt, while Octavian landed in Epirus and camped north of the Gulf of Ambracia. Antony's army, trapped at Actium, suffered disease, hunger and desertions. On 2 September Antony's fleet broke out; Cleopatra and Antony escaped to Egypt with sixty ships and the treasury, but most of the fleet was destroyed or surrendered, and the army capitulated a week later.

In 30 Octavian invaded Egypt from Syria and Gallus from Cyrenaica. Antony's forces deserted. On 1 August Octavian entered Alexandria; Antony killed himself, and Cleopatra followed some days later. Caesarion was executed, and Egypt annexed.

The war ended the civil wars and left Octavian sole ruler of the Roman world. Augustan propaganda made Actium the victory of Rome, its gods and Apollo against the East and Egypt's animal gods. In 27 he became Augustus.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Antony and Cleopatra (2010)
Murray and Petsas, Octavian's Campsite Memorial for the Actian War (1989)

set.detail:
Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus was born about 163, son of the consul and censor of the same name, who had pacified Celtiberia and Sardinia, and of Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus. Raised by his mother after his father's death, with Greek tutors including Diophanes of Mytilene and the Stoic Blossius of Cumae, he married Claudia, daughter of Appius Claudius Pulcher, princeps senatus. As a young officer he was first over the wall at Carthage in 146 under his brother-in-law Scipio Aemilianus. As quaestor in Spain in 137 he negotiated, on the strength of his father's reputation among the Celtiberians, the treaty that saved the army of Hostilius Mancinus at Numantia; the Senate repudiated it, an humiliation that, Plutarch says, embittered him.

His tribunate of 133 and its land law, the deposition of Octavius, the proposal to use Attalus' bequest, and his bid for re-election led to his murder on the Capitol by senators led by his cousin Scipio Nasica. He was about thirty. His body was thrown into the Tiber.

Ancient judgments of Tiberius split along political lines. Cicero, depending on the audience, called him a seditious tribune or praised his eloquence and the nobility of his intentions; Velleius admired his character but condemned his methods; Appian and Plutarch present him with sympathy. Scipio Aemilianus, hearing of his death, quoted Homer: 'So perish anyone else who does such things'.

Modern assessments vary between Tiberius as a principled reformer (Stockton, Bernstein), an ambitious aristocrat using popular causes for faction (Badian discusses both), and a man of his class whose methods outran his intentions. His legacy is clear: he showed that the tribunate and the assembly could be used against the Senate, and his violent death opened a century of political bloodshed.

scholarship: Bernstein, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus: Tradition and Apostasy (1978)

set.detail:
Gaius Sempronius Gracchus, born about 154, was nine years younger than Tiberius and served on his brother's land commission from 133. He served at Numantia under Scipio Aemilianus and as quaestor in Sardinia (126-124), where he won goodwill by persuading local communities to supply the army's clothing. Plutarch says Tiberius appeared to him in a dream, telling him he would share his fate. He was the greatest orator of his time, fiery and theatrical, and Cicero, despite his politics, judged him a loss to Latin letters.

His tribunates of 123 and 122 produced a programme of unprecedented breadth: grain distribution at a subsidised price, colonies at Tarentum, Capua and Carthage (Junonia), roads, the transfer of extortion juries to the equites, the farming of Asian taxes in Rome, laws on provinces, the army and capital trials, and a proposal to enfranchise the Latins. He organised the work personally, inspecting roads and building granaries. His absence in Africa founding Junonia and the Senate's use of Livius Drusus to outbid him undermined his support.

Failing to win a third tribunate, he was drawn into the confrontation with the consul Opimius over the repeal of the Junonia law. After the senatus consultum ultimum he and Fulvius Flaccus occupied the Aventine; when it was stormed, he fled across the Tiber and was killed, at his own wish, by his slave in the grove of Furrina. Some 3,000 supporters died.

Gaius was more radical and more systematic than his brother, and his programme set the agenda of popularis politics for a century. His reforms transformed the equites into a political class and established the state grain supply. His fate taught the next generations that reform through the assemblies against the Senate's will invited death.

scholarship: Sherwin-White, 'The lex repetundarum and the political ideas of Gaius Gracchus', JRS 72 (1982)

set.detail:
Cornelia, younger daughter of Scipio Africanus and Aemilia, was born about 190 and married Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, consul 177 and 163, a man some twenty-five years older. She bore twelve children, of whom three survived to adulthood: Tiberius, Gaius and Sempronia, who married Scipio Aemilianus. After her husband's death in about 154 she refused remarriage, including, it was said, an offer from Ptolemy VIII of Egypt, and devoted herself to her children's education, hiring the best Greek teachers.

Valerius Maximus tells the famous story that when a Campanian lady displayed her jewels and asked to see Cornelia's, she presented her sons: 'These are my jewels.' Whether or not true, the anecdote made her the model Roman mother, the univira who lived for her children. After Gaius' death she retired to a villa at Misenum, where she received Greek scholars and kings and spoke of her sons' deaths, Plutarch says, without tears, as if of ancient heroes.

Cicero read her letters and praised their style; Quintilian names her as an example of women's eloquence shaping their sons. Two fragments of a letter to Gaius, urging him not to stand for the tribunate, are preserved in the manuscripts of Cornelius Nepos; their authenticity is debated, some seeing a later forgery. After her death, a bronze statue was erected in her honour in the Porticus of Metellus, later of Octavia; its base, inscribed 'Cornelia, daughter of Africanus, mother of the Gracchi', survives and was likely the first public statue of a Roman woman.

Cornelia became an icon of Roman womanhood, celebrated by later generations and especially by Augustus, who restored her statue. Her letters make her one of the few Roman women whose voice may survive.
set.debate: Authenticity of the letter fragments transmitted with Nepos is debated.

scholarship: Dixon, Cornelia: Mother of the Gracchi (2007)
Hallett, Fathers and Daughters in Roman Society (1984)

set.detail:
Jugurtha, born about 160, was the illegitimate son of Mastanabal, a son of Masinissa, and grew up at the court of his uncle Micipsa, king of Numidia. Sallust portrays him as handsome, intelligent, athletic and popular, a skilled hunter and horseman. Micipsa, fearing his popularity, sent him in 134 with a Numidian contingent to serve under Scipio Aemilianus at Numantia, hoping he would die; instead he won distinction and Roman friends, who, Sallust says, told him that at Rome anything could be bought. Micipsa adopted him and made him co-heir with his sons Adherbal and Hiempsal.

After Micipsa's death in 118, Jugurtha had Hiempsal murdered and drove out Adherbal. The Senate divided Numidia in 116, giving Jugurtha the richer west. In 112 he besieged Adherbal in Cirta and massacred its Italian defenders, provoking war with Rome. He bribed commanders, came to Rome under safe conduct in 111 and had his cousin Massiva murdered there. He defeated Aulus Albinus at Suthul (110), and fought Metellus and Marius with a mobile guerrilla war, using Numidian cavalry and desert fortresses. In 108 he allied with his father-in-law Bocchus of Mauretania.

Betrayed by Bocchus to Sulla in 105, he walked in Marius' triumph on 1 January 104 and died in the Tullianum, by starvation or strangling, within days.

Sallust's portrait, the core of the Bellum Iugurthinum, makes Jugurtha a man of great ability corrupted by ambition and by Roman venality. Modern historians see him as a capable ruler exploiting Roman divisions to unify Numidia, a predecessor of later North African resistance to Rome, and the catalyst of the careers of Marius and Sulla.

scholarship: Kraus, 'Jugurthine disorder', in Kraus (ed.), The Limits of Historiography (1999)

set.detail:
Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus, born about 160, belonged to the most powerful family of his generation: between 123 and 109 six Caecilii Metelli held the consulship. He was a man of old-fashioned integrity and a skilled orator in the Stoic style. Consul in 109, he took command against Jugurtha after the scandals of his predecessors and restored discipline to the demoralised army, forbidding camp followers and luxuries. He won the battle of the Muthul, took Thala, and laid waste Numidia, but could not capture Jugurtha.

His legate Marius, whom he had snubbed by refusing him leave to stand for the consulship, undermined him with the equites and the people. In 107 the assembly transferred his command to Marius, an affront he never forgave. He returned to celebrate a triumph and the cognomen Numidicus.

As censor in 102 he tried to expel the tribune Saturninus and Glaucia from the Senate and to refuse the census registration of Lucius Equitius, a pretended son of Tiberius Gracchus; his colleague, his cousin, blocked him. In 100 he alone among senators refused to swear to obey Saturninus' agrarian law, declaring it illegal, and went into voluntary exile at Rhodes and Tralles, where he studied philosophy and attended lectures. His son, Quintus Metellus Pius, campaigned for his recall, passed in 98 despite Marius' opposition; the son earned his cognomen Pius for his devotion.

Metellus became for later optimates the model of the upright aristocrat persecuted by demagogues. He died about 91, rumoured to have been poisoned by Quintus Varius. Fragments of his speeches, including one urging marriage (often attributed to Metellus Macedonicus), survive in Gellius.

scholarship: Gruen, Roman Politics and the Criminal Courts, 149-78 BC (1968)

set.detail:
Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, born about 163 into an impoverished patrician family (his father dealt in charcoal, Valerius Maximus says), rose by ability and the patronage of the Metelli, whose daughter Caecilia Metella he married. Consul in 115, he triumphed over Ligurian and Carnic tribes, passed a sumptuary law, and became princeps senatus, holding that dignity until his death about 89. Censor in 109, he built the Pons Mulvius and the Via Aemilia Scauri through Etruria and Liguria.

Scaurus dominated the Senate for a generation. Sallust, hostile, depicts him as a corrupt noble who took Jugurtha's bribes while posing as an upright statesman, serving on the embassy to Jugurtha in 112 and as legate to Bestia in 111. He escaped the Mamilian commission by getting himself elected one of its presidents. He was repeatedly prosecuted, for extortion, for treason, under the lex Varia, and always acquitted; in 90, before the Varian court, he answered with the famous single sentence: 'Quintus Varius of Sucro says Scaurus took bribes; Scaurus denies it; which do you believe?'

He supported Livius Drusus in 91 and urged the Senate's resistance to Saturninus in 100, joining the armed force against him. He wrote an autobiography in three books, used by later historians, and was a patron of Cicero's teachers. Cicero, unlike Sallust, admired him as a model statesman of gravitas.

His widow Caecilia Metella married Sulla, and his son Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, praetor 56 and aedile 58, gave the most lavish games in Roman history, with a theatre of 3,000 statues, and was defended by Cicero in 54.

scholarship: Gruen, Roman Politics and the Criminal Courts (1968)

set.detail:
Gaius Marius was born in 157 at Cereatae near Arpinum to an equestrian family, and served with distinction at Numantia under Scipio Aemilianus, who predicted his greatness. A novus homo, he rose with the patronage of the Metelli: tribune in 119, when he passed a law narrowing the voting gangways and threatened the consul with prison; praetor in 115, narrowly escaping a bribery conviction; governor of Further Spain. He married Julia, aunt of Julius Caesar, gaining patrician connections.

As legate of Metellus in Numidia, he won the consulship of 107 and the command against Jugurtha, enrolling the capite censi; his quaestor Sulla captured Jugurtha in 105. After Arausio he was elected consul five times in succession (104-100), trained a new army, and destroyed the Teutones at Aquae Sextiae (102) and, with Catulus, the Cimbri at Vercellae (101). Hailed as the third founder of Rome, he held a sixth consulship in 100, but his alliance with Saturninus ended in disaster when he had to suppress his allies under the senatus consultum ultimum.

Sidelined for a decade, he served in the Social War with moderate success. In 88 the tribune Sulpicius gave him the Mithridatic command; Sulla's march on Rome drove him into flight: hiding in the marshes of Minturnae, imprisoned, where a Gallic or Cimbric slave sent to kill him fled, saying he could not kill Gaius Marius, and exiled in Africa, sitting amid the ruins of Carthage. He returned with Cinna in 87, took Rome, massacred his enemies, and died in January 86, early in his seventh consulship.

Plutarch's Life, drawing on hostile sources including Sulla's memoirs, presents Marius as a great soldier undone by ambition and resentment. Modern scholars debate his military reforms, his political skill, and his responsibility for the militarisation of politics.

scholarship: Carney, A Biography of C. Marius (1961)

set.detail:
Lucius Appuleius Saturninus, of a praetorian family, was quaestor at Ostia in 104, where he was removed from charge of the grain supply during a shortage and replaced by Scaurus; Cicero says this turned him toward popular politics. Tribune in 103, he carried laws allotting land in Africa to Marius' veterans and creating a new court for treason (maiestas, the 'diminution of the majesty of the Roman people'), used against the generals responsible for the Cimbric disasters. He secured Marius' fourth consulship.

Re-elected tribune for 100 after the murder of a rival candidate, he allied with the praetor Gaius Servilius Glaucia and Marius. He carried a law settling Marius' veterans in Transalpine Gaul and founding colonies in Sicily, Achaea and Macedonia, with Marius empowered to grant citizenship to three Italians in each colony, and requiring senators to swear obedience; Metellus Numidicus refused and went into exile. He may also have carried a grain law and a law on praetorian provinces, known from inscriptions at Delphi and Cnidus, which ordered measures against piracy and required oaths from magistrates.

In the elections for 99, Gaius Memmius, a consular candidate rival to Glaucia, was clubbed to death. The Senate passed the senatus consultum ultimum; Marius, as consul, besieged Saturninus and Glaucia on the Capitol. They surrendered on promises of safety, but were killed in the Senate house by a mob that stripped the roof tiles. Thirty-seven years later Caesar and Labienus prosecuted the elderly Rabirius for his murder.

Saturninus is portrayed in the sources, mostly hostile, as a violent demagogue. Modern scholars, notably Badian, see him as a serious politician whose programme addressed veterans' settlement and the empire's administration, destroyed by the collapse of his alliance with Marius.

scholarship: Badian, 'The death of Saturninus', Chiron 14 (1984)
Crawford (ed.), Roman Statutes (1996) no. 12

set.detail:
Marcus Livius Drusus, born about 124, was the son of the tribune who opposed Gaius Gracchus in 122 and became consul in 112. Wealthy, proud and eloquent, he was connected by marriage to the Servilii Caepiones (his sister Livia married Quintus Servilius Caepio and later Marcus Porcius Cato, making him the uncle of Cato the Younger and of Servilia). He grew up in the circle of Crassus the orator and Scaurus. When an architect offered to build him a house hidden from view, he told him to build one where all his actions could be seen.

As tribune in 91, he presented a programme to settle the conflicts of the age: the Senate would be enlarged by 300 equites and recover the courts; colonies and grain distribution would satisfy the plebs; and citizenship would be given to the Italian allies. His laws provoked opposition from the equites, from Italian landowners threatened by his agrarian laws, and from the consul Philippus, who attacked him in the Senate. Drusus, Florus says, threatened to have Philippus strangled. The Senate annulled his laws, and he was murdered in his house in autumn 91 by an unknown assassin with a shoemaker's knife.

His close ties with the Italian leaders, especially the Marsic Poppaedius Silo, who stayed at his house, and the oath of loyalty attributed to them by Diodorus, show that the allies saw him as their champion. His death triggered the Social War.

Ancient writers present Drusus variously: Velleius as a noble reformer, Florus and Appian as an ambitious demagogue. His nephew Cato admired him. His adopted son, Marcus Livius Drusus Claudianus, was the father of Livia, wife of Augustus, through whom his name passed into the imperial family.

scholarship: Gabba, Republican Rome: The Army and the Allies (1976)

set.detail:
Quintus Poppaedius (or Pompaedius) Silo was the leader of the Marsi, the most warlike of the central Italian peoples, of whom Romans said there was no triumph over them nor without them. He was a guest-friend of Marcus Livius Drusus and stayed at his house in Rome in 91, where, Plutarch tells, he jokingly dangled the young Cato out of a window to make him support the Italians' cause; the boy refused. Diodorus says that before Drusus' tribunate he led 10,000 Marsi toward Rome with concealed weapons, intending to force the Senate, but was persuaded to turn back by a Roman, Gnaeus Domitius.

After Drusus' murder, Silo became one of the two consuls of the Italian confederation, commanding the northern front. In 90 he won several victories, notably ambushing and killing the Roman commander Quintus Servilius Caepio by pretending to desert to him with his sons as hostages and lead ingots plated with gold and silver. Coins of the confederation bear his name in Latin, Q. SILO. Marius defeated the Marsi later that year, and the Marsi surrendered in 89.

Silo continued the war in the south. He recaptured Bovianum, entering it in triumph, but in 88 he was defeated and killed in Apulia by the praetor Quintus Metellus Pius. The Romans said that the war was a war 'of the Marsi', bellum Marsicum, in recognition of his role.

Silo personified the paradox of the Social War: a man who knew Rome intimately, friend of its aristocrats, fighting it with Roman methods for the right to belong to it. He did not live to see the citizenship granted to all Italians that the war secured.

scholarship: Dart, The Social War, 91 to 88 BCE (2014)
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967)

set.detail:
Lucius Cornelius Sulla was born in 138 into an old patrician family that had fallen into obscurity and poverty; he grew up in a rented flat and spent his youth with actors and musicians. Legacies from his stepmother and a mistress, Nicopolis, allowed him to enter politics. As Marius' quaestor in Numidia he negotiated Jugurtha's capture (105); he fought under Marius and Catulus against the Cimbri, governed Cilicia (about 96 or 92), where he installed Ariobarzanes and met the first Parthian envoy, and distinguished himself in the Social War, winning the grass crown and the consulship of 88.

Deprived of the Mithridatic command by Sulpicius' law, he marched on Rome, the first general to do so. In Greece he sacked Athens and destroyed Mithridates' armies at Chaeronea and Orchomenus, made the peace of Dardanus, and returned in 83 to win the civil war, culminating at the Colline Gate. As dictator from 82 he proscribed thousands, settled veterans in colonies, and reformed the constitution to make the Senate supreme. He took the cognomen Felix and named his twins Faustus and Fausta. In 79 he retired, and died in 78 at Puteoli.

Sulla's character fascinated ancient writers. Sallust describes him as learned in Greek and Latin literature, eloquent, generous, a master of dissimulation. His face, blotched red and white, was compared to a mulberry sprinkled with meal. He was devoted to his fortune and to Venus and Apollo. His twenty-two books of memoirs shaped the tradition.

Modern assessments range from a reactionary tyrant to the last defender of the Republic (Keaveney). His legacy was paradoxical: he restored senatorial government, but showed every successor how to seize power with an army.

scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (1982, 2nd ed. 2005)
Flower, Roman Republics (2010)

set.detail:
Lucius Cornelius Cinna, of a patrician family, served as a legate in the Social War, receiving the surrender of the Marsi. Elected consul for 87 with Sulla's acquiescence, after swearing to respect Sulla's acts, he immediately revived Sulpicius' proposal to distribute the new citizens among all the tribes. His colleague Gnaeus Octavius drove him out of Rome after fighting in the Forum, and the Senate deposed him, an unprecedented act.

Cinna appealed to the army at Nola, which swore loyalty to him, and to the Italian towns, raising money and troops. He recalled Marius from Africa and, with Carbo and Sertorius, besieged and took Rome in late 87. Though Marius' massacres were committed in his name, Cinna and Sertorius eventually suppressed Marius' slave bodyguard. He held the consulship four times in succession (87-84), the first two with Marius and then Carbo, without proper elections.

The 'Cinnan regime' (dominatio Cinnae, in Cicero's phrase) has a poor reputation in the sources, which derive largely from Sullan propaganda. Yet it restored stability, enrolled the new citizens in all thirty-five tribes, passed debt relief, and supported Marius Gratidianus' coinage reform. Many nobles cooperated with it. It sent an army under Flaccus against Mithridates, and declared Sulla a public enemy.

In 84, preparing to meet Sulla's return by crossing to Greece, Cinna was killed by his own soldiers at Ancona during a mutiny of troops unwilling to embark. His daughter Cornelia married Julius Caesar, who refused Sulla's order to divorce her. His son Lucius Cornelius Cinna was praetor in 44 and praised the assassins.

scholarship: Lovano, The Age of Cinna: Crucible of Late Republican Rome (2002)

set.detail:
Mithridates VI Eupator Dionysus, born about 135 at Sinope, was the son of Mithridates V of Pontus and Laodice, a Seleucid princess. After his father's murder in about 120 he survived intrigues, according to legend hiding in the wilderness for seven years, and seized power around 113, imprisoning his mother and killing his brother. He claimed descent from Darius and Alexander, presenting himself as heir of Persian and Macedonian kingship.

He built an empire around the Black Sea: the Crimea and the Bosporan kingdom, through his general Diophantus, defending the Greek cities from the Scythians, Colchis, Lesser Armenia, and parts of Paphlagonia, Cappadocia and Galatia. He allied with Tigranes of Armenia, marrying his daughter Cleopatra to him. His rivalry with Rome's clients brought three wars: in the first (89-85) he overran Asia and ordered the massacre of the Italians, but was defeated by Sulla; the second (83-81) was a brief clash with Murena; in the third (73-63) he invaded Bithynia, lost his kingdom to Lucullus, fled to Armenia, recovered it, and was finally defeated by Pompey. He died in 63 at Panticapaeum.

Ancient writers were fascinated by him: his strength, his skill as a horseman, his knowledge of twenty-two languages, his library, his patronage of Greek culture, and his study of poisons and antidotes, which gave his name to the universal antidote mithridatium. He was also ruthless, killing his sons, wives and mother, and ordering massacres.

Cicero called him the greatest king since Alexander. His coins, with their idealised, windswept portrait, show a Hellenistic king modelling himself on Alexander. Modern historians see him as an able ruler who exploited Greek resentment of Rome.

scholarship: Højte (ed.), Mithridates VI and the Pontic Kingdom (2009)

set.detail:
Quintus Sertorius was born about 123 at Nursia in the Sabine country to an equestrian family, raised by his widowed mother Rhea, to whom he was devoted. He trained as an orator but turned to the army, surviving Arausio by swimming the Rhône, and serving under Marius against the Cimbri, when he spied in the enemy camp disguised as a Celt. He served in Spain under Titus Didius and in the Social War, where he lost an eye, which he wore, Plutarch says, as a badge of honour. Sulla blocked his tribunate candidacy, and he joined Cinna in 87, though he opposed Marius' massacres.

Sent to Spain in 83, he was driven out in 81, fled to Mauretania, and in 80 accepted the Lusitanians' invitation to lead them. For eight years he defeated Roman armies under Metellus Pius and Pompey, creating a Roman government in exile with a senate of emigrés, and training Spanish troops in Roman discipline. He won Iberian loyalty with a white fawn he claimed was a gift of Diana, and founded a school at Osca for the sons of Spanish nobles. In 75 he allied with Mithridates. His reverses after 75 made him suspicious and harsh, and in 73 or 72 he was murdered at a banquet by his lieutenant Perperna.

Plutarch paired him with Eumenes as a great general fighting abroad for a lost cause, and stressed his gentleness and respect for his mother; Sallust's lost Histories made him a central figure. He was compared to Hannibal for his loss of an eye and his guerrilla genius.

Modern historians debate whether he aimed at restoring the Marian Republic in Rome, as his senate suggests, or at an independent Spain. His war trained Pompey and shaped Spanish loyalties for a generation.

Lucius Licinius Lucullus, born about 118, was the son of the praetor convicted after the Sicilian slave war and a Caecilia Metella. He and his brother Marcus began their careers by prosecuting their father's accuser. He served under Sulla in the Social War and was the only officer to follow him in the march on Rome in 88; as quaestor and proquaestor in the East he minted Sulla's coinage, collected a fleet, won at Tenedos, and administered the fine on Asia. Sulla dedicated his memoirs to him and made him guardian of his son.

Consul in 74, he took command against Mithridates, relieved Cyzicus by starving the besieging army, conquered Pontus, and in 69 invaded Armenia, winning a stunning victory at Tigranocerta against odds. He relieved the cities of Asia from crushing debts, limiting interest to 12 per cent and capping repayments at a quarter of income, which earned the hatred of the equestrian moneylenders. His strict discipline and refusal to permit looting alienated his soldiers, who mutinied in 68 under the influence of his brother-in-law Clodius. Stripped of his provinces, he was superseded by Pompey in 66 and waited three years outside Rome for his triumph, celebrated in 63.

He then largely withdrew from politics, opposing Pompey's eastern acts, and devoted himself to luxury: his gardens on the Pincian, his villas at Tusculum and Naples, with fishponds cut through mountains (Pompey called him 'Xerxes in a toga'), and banquets in the Apollo room. He introduced the cherry to Italy from Cerasus. He assembled a great library open to scholars, and patronised the poet Archias and the philosopher Antiochus. He died in 57, mentally deranged.

Plutarch's Life paired him with Cimon. Modern historians rate him as one of the ablest Roman generals.

Tigranes II, the Great, born about 140, was a member of the Artaxiad dynasty of Armenia who spent his youth as a hostage at the Parthian court of Mithridates II, being released in about 95 on ceding seventy valleys. He became king of Armenia and built an empire. He married Cleopatra, daughter of Mithridates VI of Pontus, and allied with him, conquered Sophene, invaded Cappadocia, and took advantage of Parthia's weakness after Mithridates II's death to annex Atropatene, Gordyene, Adiabene and northern Mesopotamia, recovering the seventy valleys. In 83 he occupied Syria, ending the Seleucid civil wars, and Cilicia, and ruled to the borders of Egypt and Judaea. He took the title 'King of Kings'.

He founded a new capital, Tigranocerta, populated with Greeks, Cilicians and others deported from Cappadocia and Mesopotamia, and had four vassal kings attend him on foot. His court was Hellenised; his coins show him wearing the Armenian tiara with stars and eagles.

In 71 he refused Lucullus' demand to surrender Mithridates. Lucullus defeated him at Tigranocerta in 69 and on the Arsanias in 68. When Pompey invaded in 66, Tigranes, facing a revolt by his son Tigranes the Younger supported by Parthia, surrendered at Artaxata, laying his diadem at Pompey's feet. Pompey restored it, leaving him Armenia proper but taking Syria, Cilicia and Sophene, and demanding 6,000 talents. Tigranes remained a loyal ally until his death about 55.

Tigranes is remembered in Armenian historical memory as the greatest king, who made Armenia briefly the strongest power in western Asia. Plutarch's Lucullus depicts him as arrogant and vain.

scholarship: Manandyan, Tigranes II and Rome (trans. 2007)

set.detail:
Spartacus was a Thracian, probably from the Maedi of the Strymon valley. Appian says he had served as a soldier with the Romans, presumably as an auxiliary, then deserted or rebelled, was captured and sold as a gladiator. Plutarch describes him as intelligent and humane, more Greek than his origins suggested, and says his wife, a prophetess of Dionysus from his tribe, saw a snake coil round his face as he slept, a sign of great and terrible power. His name may relate to Thracian royal names (Spartokos of the Bosporan dynasty).

In 73 he escaped with some seventy gladiators from the school of Lentulus Batiatus at Capua, led the revolt with Crixus and Oenomaus, and defeated two praetorian armies and both consuls of 72 and the governor of Cisalpine Gaul. His army reached tens of thousands. Sources say he shared booty equally, forbade the use of gold and silver in his camp, and trained his men in Roman methods; he also sacrificed 300 Roman prisoners at Crixus' funeral as gladiatorial combats. He defeated the consuls in Picenum and marched to the Alps, but turned south, either because his followers refused to leave Italy or to attack Rome. Trapped in Bruttium by Crassus' wall, he broke through, but was defeated and killed at the Silarus in 71. His body was never found.

The ancient tradition, though hostile to slave revolt, credited him with ability and personal courage. Sallust, Plutarch and Appian present him sympathetically. From the eighteenth century he became a hero of liberty: Voltaire admired him; Marx called him a genuine representative of the ancient proletariat; he inspired Khachaturian's ballet and Kubrick's film.

Modern historians stress that there is no evidence he aimed to abolish slavery, and that his aims remain uncertain.

scholarship: Urbainczyk, Spartacus (2004)

set.detail:
Marcus Licinius Crassus, born about 115, son of the censor Publius Crassus who died in the Marian massacres of 87, fled to Spain, hid in a cave for eight months, then raised an army and joined Sulla in 83. He won the decisive right wing at the Colline Gate. He built a huge fortune by buying proscribed estates cheaply, by real estate speculation, buying burning buildings and those next to them at low prices and rebuilding them with a private fire brigade of slaves, and by mines and slave training. Plutarch estimated his fortune at 7,100 talents; Crassus said no one was rich who could not maintain an army from his income.

Praetor in 73, he received the command against Spartacus, restored discipline by decimation, and defeated and killed him in 71, crucifying 6,000 prisoners along the Via Appia. He resented Pompey's claim to have finished the war. Consul with Pompey in 70, they restored the tribunes' powers. Through the 60s he built a political network by lending money to senators, defending them in court, and backing Caesar, whose debts he guaranteed before he left for Spain in 61. As censor in 65 he proposed annexing Egypt. He was suspected of involvement in Catiline's plots.

In 60 he joined Pompey and Caesar in the coalition that dominated politics. Consul again in 55, he took Syria for five years, plundered the Jerusalem Temple, and invaded Parthia; his army was destroyed at Carrhae in 53, and he was killed at a parley. Dio reports the story that the Parthians poured molten gold into his mouth to mock his greed; Plutarch has his head used as a prop in a performance of the Bacchae.

Crassus has been seen as a plutocrat consumed by jealousy of Pompey; Ward and Marshall present him as a shrewd politician who used his wealth to build support.

scholarship: Marshall, Crassus: A Political Biography (1976)

set.detail:
Gnaeus Pompeius, born on 29 September 106, was the son of Pompeius Strabo, the hated Picene general of the Social War, under whom he served at Asculum, appearing on the bronze recording Strabo's council. In 83, aged twenty-three, he raised three legions privately in Picenum and joined Sulla, who greeted him as imperator. He crushed the Marians in Sicily and Africa, earning the name Magnus and a triumph in 81 as an eques. He helped suppress Lepidus in 77 and spent 77-71 in Spain against Sertorius, then shared the consulship of 70 with Crassus without having held any previous office, restoring the tribunate.

The lex Gabinia (67) gave him command against the pirates, whom he cleared in three months; the lex Manilia (66) the war against Mithridates. In four years he defeated Mithridates, received Tigranes' surrender, campaigned to the Caucasus, annexed Syria, took Jerusalem, founded cities, and reorganised the East, celebrating a magnificent triumph in 61. Frustrated by the Senate's refusal to ratify his acts, he allied with Caesar and Crassus in 60, marrying Caesar's daughter Julia. He held the cura annonae from 57, a second consulship in 55, Spain by legates, and the sole consulship of 52, restoring order after Clodius' murder.

After Julia's death (54) and Crassus' (53) he drifted toward the optimates, marrying Cornelia, daughter of Metellus Scipio, and became the Senate's champion against Caesar. In 49 he abandoned Italy, beat Caesar at Dyrrachium, but lost at Pharsalus, and was murdered on landing in Egypt in September 48, the day after his fifty-eighth birthday.

Ancient writers judged him variously: vain, sensitive to praise, a poor politician but a superb organiser. Sallust called him 'modest in face, shameless in mind'. Modern historians (Seager, Gelzer) see him as the archetype of the extraordinary commander whose career foreshadowed the Principate, yet who sought recognition within the Republic.

scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great: A Political Biography (2nd ed. 2002)
Leach, Pompey the Great (1978)

set.detail:
Lucius Sergius Catilina, born about 108 into an ancient but faded patrician family that claimed descent from Sergestus, a companion of Aeneas, served on Pompeius Strabo's staff at Asculum in 89. Under Sulla he was a killer during the proscriptions, accused of murdering his brother-in-law and parading the head of Marius Gratidianus through the city. He was acquitted in 73 of seducing the Vestal Fabia, Terentia's half-sister. Praetor in 68, governor of Africa in 67-66, he was prosecuted for extortion and prevented from standing for the consulship of 65. He was linked, probably falsely, to a 'first conspiracy' to murder the consuls in 65.

Defeated in 64 by Cicero and Antonius, and again in 63 for 62, he turned to revolution, promising debt cancellation to the indebted and dispossessed: Sullan veterans, bankrupt nobles, and Etruscan peasants. His ally Manlius raised an army in Etruria; Cicero drove Catiline from Rome in November 63 and exposed his accomplices, who were executed. Catiline joined Manlius' army and died fighting at Pistoria in January 62, found far ahead of his men among enemy dead, still breathing, his face retaining the ferocity of life.

Sallust's portrait is the classic study of a corrupt but gifted aristocrat: 'great strength of mind and body, but an evil and depraved nature'. Cicero's Catilinarians made him the archetypal enemy of the state. Yet in Pro Caelio Cicero admitted that Catiline had many qualities that attracted good men.

Modern historians debate the reality of the conspiracy and Catiline's aims. Some see a genuine social movement of the indebted; others the desperate gamble of a failed aristocrat, inflated by Cicero's self-promotion.

scholarship: Levick, Catiline (2015)

set.detail:
Marcus Tullius Cicero, born on 3 January 106 at Arpinum to an equestrian family, studied in Rome under the jurists Scaevola and the orators Crassus and Antonius, and philosophy with Philo of Larissa, Diodotus and later Antiochus, Posidonius and Molon. He made his name defending Sextus Roscius of Ameria against Sulla's freedman (80), and established his supremacy with the prosecution of Verres (70). A novus homo, he rose through each office at the earliest legal age, culminating in the consulship of 63, when he suppressed Catiline's conspiracy and executed five conspirators without trial, earning the title pater patriae.

He declined to join the coalition of 60, was exiled in 58 by Clodius for the executions, recalled in 57, and then forced to support the dynasts after Luca. He governed Cilicia (51-50), joined Pompey reluctantly in 49, was pardoned by Caesar after Pharsalus, and withdrew into writing, producing in 46-44 the bulk of his philosophy. After the Ides he led the Senate against Antony with the Philippics, backing Octavian; he was proscribed and murdered on 7 December 43.

Cicero's surviving works are vast: 58 speeches, rhetorical treatises (De oratore, Brutus, Orator), philosophical works (De re publica, De legibus, De finibus, Tusculans, De natura deorum, De officiis), poetry, and over 900 letters to Atticus, his brother, and friends, giving an unrivalled view of the period. His prose became the model of Latin style.

Judgments of Cicero have swung between admiration for his humanity and eloquence (Petrarch, the Enlightenment) and contempt for his vanity and vacillation (Mommsen). Modern historians stress his commitment to the Republic and to concord between the orders.

scholarship: Rawson, Cicero: A Portrait (1975)
Mitchell, Cicero: The Ascending Years (1979) and The Senior Statesman (1991)
Everitt, Cicero (2001)

set.detail:
Marcus Porcius Cato, great-grandson of Cato the Censor, was born in 95 and orphaned young; he was raised in the house of his uncle Marcus Livius Drusus, tribune of 91. A Stoic from youth, he cultivated austerity: walking barefoot, bareheaded, wearing dark clothes, drinking heavily with philosophers. As quaestor in 64 he reformed the treasury, prosecuting corrupt clerks and recovering Sulla's bounties from proscription killers. As tribune-designate in 63 he swayed the Senate to execute the Catilinarians with a speech that Sallust paired with Caesar's.

He became the moral leader of the optimates, opposing Pompey's eastern acts, the tax-farmers' remission, Caesar's triumph and consulship, filibustering whenever possible. As tribune in 62 he extended the grain dole. Clodius removed him in 58 by sending him to annex Cyprus, which he did with scrupulous honesty, bringing 7,000 talents to the treasury. He opposed the lex Trebonia, was praetor in 54 after losing in 55, and lost the consular election of 51. In 52 he supported Pompey's sole consulship as the lesser evil.

In 49 he joined Pompey, put on mourning, and refused to shave or cut his hair. After Pharsalus he led the remnant fleet to Africa, marching his army across the Libyan desert, and commanded Utica during the Thapsus campaign. After Thapsus he killed himself, refusing Caesar's pardon, in April 46.

Cato's death made him a martyr: Cicero's Cato, Brutus' eulogy, Caesar's Anticato, Lucan, Seneca, and later Addison and the American revolutionaries. Cicero, however, complained he acted as if he lived in Plato's Republic rather than Romulus' cesspit, and modern historians see his intransigence as having pushed Pompey and Caesar together and made compromise impossible.

scholarship: Goar, The Legend of Cato Uticensis (1987)
Morrell, Pompey, Cato, and the Governance of the Roman Empire (2017)

set.detail:
Publius Clodius Pulcher, born about 93, was the youngest son of Appius Claudius Pulcher, consul 79, of the proud patrician Claudii; he used the popular spelling Clodius. Serving under his brother-in-law Lucullus in the East, he incited the army's mutiny in 68; he then served under another brother-in-law, Marcius Rex, and was captured by pirates. In 62 he disguised himself as a woman to enter the Bona Dea rites at Caesar's house, apparently to meet Caesar's wife Pompeia; he was tried for sacrilege in 61 and acquitted by a bribed jury, but Cicero's testimony demolishing his alibi made them enemies for life.

In 59 Caesar and Pompey arranged his adoption into a plebeian family so he could become tribune. In 58 his legislation made the grain dole free, restored the collegia, curbed obnuntiatio and the censors' powers, exiled Cicero, annexed Cyprus and gave Piso and Gabinius rich provinces. He organised his followers by districts through the collegia, creating a powerful urban organisation, and soon turned against Pompey, harassing him in the streets.

From 57 he fought Milo's gangs for control of the streets, opposed Cicero's recall, and as aedile in 56 prosecuted Milo. He was candidate for the praetorship of 52 when, on 18 January 52, he met Milo on the Via Appia near Bovillae and was killed in the ensuing brawl. His followers burned his body in the Senate house, which went up in flames.

Cicero, our main source, portrays Clodius as a monster of vice and violence. Modern scholars (Tatum, Benner, Vanderbroeck) see him as an aristocratic popularis politician of exceptional talent who built a lasting base among the urban plebs, independent of the triumvirs. His sisters, including Clodia, were notorious; his widow Fulvia married Curio and then Antony.

scholarship: Benner, Die Politik des P. Clodius Pulcher (1987)
Vanderbroeck, Popular Leadership and Collective Behavior in the Late Roman Republic (1987)

set.detail:
Gaius Julius Caesar was born on 12 or 13 July 100 into an old patrician family claiming descent from Venus through Aeneas' son Iulus, but of modest recent distinction; his aunt Julia was Marius' wife. Married to Cinna's daughter Cornelia, he defied Sulla's order to divorce her. He served in Asia, won the civic crown at Mytilene, was captured by pirates and later crucified them, and studied rhetoric at Rhodes. He climbed the cursus with spectacular expenditure: as aedile in 65 he restored Marius' trophies; in 63 he won the election for pontifex maximus against Catulus and argued against executing the Catilinarians. After his praetorship (62) and governorship of Further Spain (61-60), he formed the coalition with Pompey and Crassus.

As consul in 59 he forced through legislation against his colleague Bibulus, and obtained Gaul and Illyricum. In nine years (58-50) he conquered Gaul, crossed the Rhine, invaded Britain, and crushed Vercingetorix at Alesia, accumulating wealth, a devoted army and glory. Refused a second consulship on his terms, he crossed the Rubicon in January 49, and in four years defeated the Pompeians in Italy, Spain, Greece, Egypt, Asia, Africa and Spain again. Dictator from 49, perpetual dictator from early 44, he passed reforms including the Julian calendar, colonies, debt measures, citizenship grants and the reduction of the grain dole, and pardoned enemies. He was assassinated on 15 March 44 by senators led by Brutus and Cassius, many of whom he had spared.

Caesar was also a great writer: his Commentaries on the Gallic and Civil Wars are masterpieces of plain style and propaganda. Ancient writers admired his speed, clemency and genius, while condemning his ambition. Modern judgments range from Mommsen's ideal statesman to a ruthless aristocrat whose ambition destroyed the Republic.

scholarship: Meier, Caesar (1982, trans. 1995)

set.detail:
Titus Labienus, born about 100 in Picenum, probably at Cingulum, came from a region dominated by the Pompeii and was likely a client of Pompey. As tribune in 63, in cooperation with Caesar, he prosecuted the aged senator Gaius Rabirius for the murder of Saturninus, whose death had cost his uncle his life, a case designed to challenge the senatus consultum ultimum. He also restored the popular election of priests, enabling Caesar's election as pontifex maximus.

From 58 to 50 he was Caesar's senior legate in Gaul, second in command, often entrusted with independent operations: he defeated the Tigurini at the Arar, held the left at the Sabis and turned the battle, defeated Indutiomarus and the Treveri, conquered the Parisii at Lutetia in 52 while Caesar was at Gergovia, and played a key role at Alesia. Caesar left him in charge of Cisalpine Gaul in 50. He grew enormously rich, building a town at Cingulum.

In January 49, within days of the Rubicon, he deserted to Pompey, perhaps out of loyalty to his old patron, perhaps resenting Caesar's dominance. Caesar sent his baggage after him. He became one of the most implacable Pompeian commanders: at Dyrrachium he executed Caesarian prisoners after taunting them; at Pharsalus he commanded the cavalry on the left whose rout decided the battle. In Africa he nearly defeated Caesar at Ruspina, and fought at Thapsus. He escaped to Spain and fell at Munda in 45; his head was brought to Caesar.

Caesar's Commentaries praise his skill, though after his defection they diminish his role. Lucan and Cicero portray him as a man of energy and ambition. His son Quintus Labienus led the Parthian invasion of 40.

scholarship: Syme, 'The allegiance of Labienus', JRS 28 (1938)

set.detail:
Vercingetorix, born about 82, was the son of Celtillus, an Arvernian noble who had been executed by his people for seeking kingship over Gaul. Caesar says he was young, of great influence, and had served Caesar as a cavalry commander. After the massacre at Cenabum in early 52 he raised his clients, was expelled from Gergovia by his uncle Gobannitio and the nobles, returned with an army of the poor and outlawed, and was proclaimed king. He secured the support of most of the peoples of central and western Gaul and was elected supreme commander, imposing strict discipline and severe punishments.

His strategy was to deny Caesar supplies by burning towns and farms and harassing foragers with cavalry. He reluctantly allowed the Bituriges to defend Avaricum, which Caesar took; he defeated Caesar at Gergovia, the only defeat Caesar suffered in person in Gaul, causing the Aedui to defect. A council at Bibracte confirmed him as commander. After his cavalry was defeated, he shut himself in Alesia with 80,000 men, while a relief army was raised. After the failure of the relief army, he surrendered, offering himself as a sacrifice for his people.

He was taken to Rome, held for six years, and displayed in Caesar's Gallic triumph in 46, then executed, probably strangled in the Tullianum. His coins, gold staters inscribed VERCINGETORIXS, show a youthful head, probably of a god.

Vercingetorix became a French national hero in the nineteenth century, celebrated by Napoleon III, who erected a statue at Alesia, and by historians such as Camille Jullian. Modern scholars see him as a Gallic aristocrat exploiting a moment of resentment, whose achievement was to unite a large part of Gaul.

scholarship: Goudineau, Le dossier Vercingétorix (2001)
Jullian, Vercingétorix (1901)

set.detail:
Cleopatra VII Philopator, born in 69, was the daughter of Ptolemy XII Auletes and perhaps Cleopatra V, of the Macedonian dynasty that had ruled Egypt since 305. Plutarch says she was the first of her line to learn Egyptian, and spoke many languages. She became queen in 51 with her brother Ptolemy XIII; driven out by his regents in 49, she returned in 48 with Caesar's support, became his lover, and after the Alexandrian War ruled with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV. She bore Caesar a son, Ptolemy Caesar (Caesarion), and visited Rome in 46-44, where Caesar placed her golden statue in the temple of Venus Genetrix.

After the Ides she returned to Egypt, had Ptolemy XIV killed and made Caesarion co-ruler. In 41 she met Antony at Tarsus, arriving on a gilded barge dressed as Aphrodite, and wintered with him in Alexandria, bearing twins, Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene, in 40; a son, Ptolemy Philadelphus, followed in 36. Antony gave her territories in Syria, Phoenicia, Cilicia, Crete and Cyrenaica, restoring much of the Ptolemaic empire, and in 34 the Donations made her 'Queen of Kings'. She financed Antony's wars, accompanied him to Greece in 32, and sailed away at Actium with the treasury. After Antony's death, she killed herself in August 30, rather than be displayed in Octavian's triumph.

Roman sources, shaped by Octavian's propaganda, portray her as a foreign seductress and threat to Rome (Horace's 'fatale monstrum'). Plutarch adds that her charm lay in her conversation more than her beauty. Egyptian sources show her as a pharaoh and benefactor of temples, and she was revered in Egypt for centuries. Modern scholars stress her ability as a ruler and diplomat preserving her kingdom's independence.

scholarship: Schiff, Cleopatra: A Life (2010)
Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001)

set.detail:
Marcus Antonius, born about 83, was the son of Marcus Antonius Creticus and Julia, a Julian, and grandson of the orator killed in 87; his stepfather Lentulus Sura was executed as a Catilinarian in 63. A dissolute youth in the company of Curio and Clodius, he served as cavalry commander under Gabinius in Judaea and Egypt (57-55), then under Caesar in Gaul from 54. As tribune in 49 he vetoed the Senate's decrees against Caesar and fled to his camp. He commanded the left wing at Pharsalus and governed Italy as Master of Horse in 48-47, crushing Dolabella's debt riots. Consul with Caesar in 44, he offered him the diadem at the Lupercalia.

After the Ides he negotiated the amnesty, then roused the people at Caesar's funeral and took control of Caesar's papers and money. Opposed by the Senate and Octavian, he besieged Decimus Brutus at Mutina and was defeated, but joined Lepidus and Plancus, and with Octavian formed the triumvirate in 43. He was the real victor at Philippi in 42. Taking the East, he met Cleopatra at Tarsus in 41, married Octavia in 40, appointed client kings including Herod, led a disastrous Parthian campaign in 36, and in 34 proclaimed the Donations of Alexandria. War with Octavian followed: defeated at Actium in 31, he killed himself at Alexandria in August 30, dying in Cleopatra's arms.

Our sources, influenced by Octavian's propaganda and Cicero's Philippics, portray Antony as a drunk, a brawler and a slave to Cleopatra. Plutarch, using sources such as Dellius and Cleopatra's doctor Olympus, gives a more nuanced portrait of a generous, brave soldier, loved by his troops, undone by passion. Modern historians (Pelling, Goldsworthy) see him as an able general and administrator of the East.

scholarship: Huzar, Mark Antony: A Biography (1978)

set.detail:
Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, born about 89, was the son of the consul of 78 who rebelled against the Senate in 77. A patrician of high birth, he supported Caesar, proposing as praetor in 49 the law that made Caesar dictator. He governed Nearer Spain (48-47), mediating in the revolt against Quintus Cassius, and was consul with Caesar in 46 and Master of Horse from 46 to 44. On the night before the Ides, Caesar dined at his house and, asked what death was best, answered 'a sudden one'. After the murder, Lepidus brought troops into the Forum and supported Antony, succeeding Caesar as pontifex maximus.

As governor of Narbonensis and Nearer Spain he negotiated with Sextus Pompey, then in May 43 joined Antony after their soldiers fraternised, and was declared a public enemy. He was a member of the triumvirate formed at Bononia, consul again in 42, and stayed in Italy during the Philippi campaign. He sacrificed his brother Paullus to the proscriptions, though Paullus escaped. Suspected of dealings with Sextus, he was given Africa in 40. In 36 he invaded Sicily with fourteen legions to fight Sextus Pompey, but after Naulochus tried to claim the island for himself; his soldiers deserted to Octavian, who walked into his camp. Stripped of his powers, he kept the office of pontifex maximus and lived in exile at Circeii until his death in 13 or 12, when Augustus succeeded him as pontifex maximus.

Ancient writers, influenced by Augustan propaganda, depict him as weak and incompetent; Velleius says he was undeserving of the fortune he had. Modern historians (Weigel) suggest he was a capable politician whose position depended on others' armies. His survival reflected Octavian's need for legitimacy.

scholarship: Weigel, Lepidus: The Tarnished Triumvir (1992)
Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)

set.detail:
Marcus Junius Brutus, born in 85, was the son of the Marcus Brutus killed by Pompey in 77 and of Servilia, Cato's half-sister and later Caesar's mistress. Adopted by his uncle Quintus Servilius Caepio, he styled himself Quintus Caepio Brutus. He studied philosophy, especially the Old Academy of Antiochus, and wrote on virtue, duties and patience. As moneyer about 54 he celebrated his ancestors Lucius Brutus, the first consul, and Servilius Ahala, killers of would-be tyrants. In Cilicia and Cyprus he lent money to Salamis at 48 per cent, enforced by cavalry, to Cicero's embarrassment.

In 49 he joined Pompey, despite Pompey having killed his father. After Pharsalus Caesar pardoned him and appointed him governor of Cisalpine Gaul (46) and urban praetor (44), and destined him for the consulship of 41. Pressed by his brother-in-law Cassius, by graffiti on his ancestor's statue ('Brutus, are you asleep?'), and by his own principles, he led the conspiracy against Caesar. After the Ides he found Rome hostile and left for the East, where he raised legions in Macedonia, sacked Xanthus, struck the EID MAR coin, and joined Cassius at Philippi. After Cassius' death in the first battle, he fought and lost the second battle and killed himself in October 42.

Brutus was admired as a man of principle: Antony called him the only conspirator who acted from honest motives. Cicero dedicated works to him and named his history of oratory after him. Dante put him in Satan's mouth; Shakespeare made him 'the noblest Roman of them all'. Modern historians (Tempest) see a philosopher trapped by his family's legend and the logic of tyrannicide.

Gaius Cassius Longinus, born about 86, of a plebeian noble family, was quaestor to Crassus in 53. After Carrhae he led the survivors to Syria, organised its defence, executed the Jewish leader Peitholaus, and in 51 ambushed and repulsed a Parthian invasion near Antigonea. As tribune in 49 he joined Pompey and commanded a fleet that burned Caesarian ships at Messana and Vibo. After Pharsalus he surrendered to Caesar, who pardoned him and made him praetor in 44, while giving the more prestigious urban praetorship to Brutus, his wife Junia Tertia's brother. He resented Caesar, though his Epicurean philosophy hardly favoured political action.

Cassius was the moving spirit of the conspiracy, recruiting Brutus and the others. Plutarch says he proposed killing Antony as well, overruled by Brutus. After the Ides he left for the East, though assigned the minor province of Cyrene. He took Syria, absorbing the legions of Caecilius Bassus and of Caesarian governors, defeated Dolabella at Laodicea, took Rhodes after defeating its fleet, and extracted huge sums from Asia, Judaea and Tarsus. He joined Brutus at Sardis and Philippi.

At the first battle of Philippi, his camp was taken by Antony; seeing horsemen approaching, and short-sighted, he believed Brutus defeated and had his freedman Pindarus kill him; it was his birthday. Brutus called him the last of the Romans.

Cassius was harsher and more practical than Brutus: a capable soldier, and, in the sources, a more personal enemy of Caesar. His family remained hostile to the Julio-Claudians. Shakespeare's 'lean and hungry look' derives from Plutarch.

scholarship: Sedley, 'The ethics of Brutus and Cassius', JRS 87 (1997)

set.detail:
Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius, born about 67, younger son of Pompey the Great and Mucia, was with his father when he was murdered at Pelusium in 48. He fled with his stepmother Cornelia, joined the Pompeians in Africa, and after Thapsus went to Spain, where after Munda he survived among the Lacetani and Celtiberians, raising forces and taking the cognomen Pius for his loyalty to his father's memory. By 44 he controlled much of Further Spain with seven legions. Lepidus negotiated a settlement, and the Senate made him commander of the fleet (praefectus classis et orae maritimae) in 43.

Proscribed under the lex Pedia, though not one of the assassins, he seized Sicily, which became a refuge for the proscribed and runaway slaves, and with Sardinia and Corsica dominated the western Mediterranean. He called himself son of Neptune, minting coins with marine imagery. His blockade caused famine in Rome, forcing the triumvirs to sign the Treaty of Misenum (39), which recognised his territories. War resumed in 38; he defeated Octavian at sea off Cumae and Tauromenium, but was decisively defeated by Agrippa at Naulochus in 36. He fled east, intrigued with Antony and Parthia, and was captured and executed at Miletus in 35.

Augustan propaganda portrayed him as a pirate leading slaves; the Res Gestae calls the war a war against pirates. Velleius calls him uncultured, a freedman among his freedmen. Modern historians (Powell, Welch) have rehabilitated him as a Republican leader who offered refuge to the proscribed and preserved his father's cause, and whose naval power nearly destroyed Octavian.

scholarship: Powell and Welch (eds.), Sextus Pompeius (2002)

set.detail:
Fulvia, born about 77, was the daughter of Marcus Fulvius Bambalio and Sempronia, possibly a descendant of Gaius Gracchus, and an heiress of great wealth. She married three of the most important popular politicians of the age: Publius Clodius, with whom she had two children, including Clodia, briefly married to Octavian; Gaius Scribonius Curio; and Mark Antony, from about 47. At Clodius' murder in 52, she displayed his body in her atrium, inciting the crowd, and testified at Milo's trial.

As Antony's wife she was active in politics. Cicero accused her of taking bribes for Antony's decrees and of watching executions at Brundisium in 44. When Antony was declared a public enemy in 43, she lobbied senators, and Atticus protected her. During the proscriptions, Dio and Appian say she had Cicero's head brought to her and pierced his tongue with her hairpin, and had a neighbour proscribed for refusing to sell her his house.

In 41, with Antony in the East, she and Lucius Antonius championed the dispossessed Italians against Octavian, raising troops; Octavian wrote obscene verses about her, and sling bullets from Perusia carry insults aimed at her. She was the first Roman woman whose image appeared on coins, as Victory on quinarii of Lugdunum, and a town in Phrygia, Eumeneia, was renamed Fulvia. After Perusia fell, she fled to Greece, where Antony met her coldly, and she died at Sicyon in 40.

Velleius said she had nothing of a woman except her body. Modern historians see her as a political actor whose power, unusual for a Roman woman, was exaggerated by hostile sources to discredit Antony.

scholarship: Schultz, Fulvia: Playing for Power at the End of the Roman Republic (2021)

set.detail:
Marcus Terentius Varro, born in 116 at Reate in the Sabine country, studied under the antiquarian Lucius Aelius Stilo in Rome and Antiochus of Ascalon in Athens. He served as Pompey's legate in the Sertorian war, the pirate war, in which he commanded the fleet between Sicily and Delos and won a naval crown, and in Spain in 49, where he surrendered to Caesar. Pardoned after Pharsalus, he was appointed by Caesar to organise a great public library, a plan abandoned after the Ides. Proscribed by Antony in 43, who coveted his villa at Casinum, he was saved by Fufius Calenus, though his library was plundered. He lived until 27, writing to the end.

Varro was the most learned Roman of the Republic: Quintilian called him the most erudite of the Romans, and Augustine said he read so much that it is a wonder he had time to write, and wrote so much that hardly anyone could read it all. He wrote some 74 works in about 620 books, on antiquities, religion, grammar, law, philosophy, geography, agriculture, music, mathematics, and the 150 Menippean Satires in mixed prose and verse. His Imagines included 700 portraits of famous men with epigrams.

Only De lingua Latina (books 5-10 of 25, partly) and Res rusticae (three books, written at eighty) survive. His Antiquitates rerum humanarum et divinarum (41 books), dedicated to Caesar, was the foundation of Roman religious scholarship, known through Augustine's City of God, which quotes it extensively to refute paganism. His chronology fixed the foundation of Rome in 753, the 'Varronian' date still in use.

Varro's work defined the Roman intellectual tradition and shaped later encyclopaedists such as Pliny, Gellius, Isidore and medieval scholars.

scholarship: Rawson, Intellectual Life in the Late Roman Republic (1985)
Volk, The Roman Republic of Letters (2021)

set.detail:
Titus Lucretius Carus is one of the most obscure great poets of antiquity. His only certain work is De rerum natura, a hexameter poem in six books expounding Epicurean philosophy, dedicated to Gaius Memmius, praetor 58. Cicero's letter to his brother of February 54 shows that the poem was circulating then. Jerome's chronicle says he was born in 94, wrote in intervals of madness caused by a love potion, killed himself at forty-four, and that Cicero edited the poem; Donatus' life of Virgil places his death in 55 on the day Virgil assumed the toga virilis. The love potion story is generally rejected as Christian polemic, and the dates are inconsistent.

The poem explains that the universe consists of atoms moving in an infinite void, that the world arose by chance and will perish, that the soul is made of atoms and dies with the body, and that the gods exist but take no interest in the world. Its purpose is to free humanity from fear of death and of the gods, which Lucretius blames for crimes such as Agamemnon's sacrifice of Iphigenia. Book 5 traces the history of civilisation; Book 6 ends with the plague of Athens, perhaps unfinished.

The poem's power lies in its imagery and argument, combining Ennian epic style with philosophical precision; Virgil's Georgics echo it ('felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas'), and Ovid predicted its immortality. A fragment from the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum appears to contain lines from it.

Lost in the Middle Ages, the poem survived in a few Carolingian manuscripts; Poggio Bracciolini's discovery in 1417 made it a key text for Renaissance and Enlightenment thought, influencing Montaigne, Gassendi and modern atomism.
set.debate: Dates of birth and death and the circumstances of death are uncertain.

scholarship: Sedley, Lucretius and the Transformation of Greek Wisdom (1998)
Gale (ed.), Oxford Readings in Lucretius (2007)
Greenblatt, The Swerve (2011)
